title: Practice: Python for data engineering
summary: 8 questions on functions, data structures, generators, exceptions, dataclasses, file encodings and pandas nullable dtypes. Practice and review, without a timer.
provenance: Prepared by Claude Code on 2026-09-24 from the AtlasNote V3 seed; original questions, no private data or third-party text. Owner review required before publication.

questions.prompt:
def add_row(row, batch=[]):
    batch.append(row)
    return batch

add_row(1)
result = add_row(2)

What is result?

options.explanation: The default list is not recreated on each call.

options.text: A TypeError, because the default is mutable.
options.explanation: Python allows it; it is a logic bug, not an error.

questions.explanation: Default values are evaluated once, when def runs, so every call that omits batch shares the same list. Use batch=None and create a new list inside the function.

links.label: Review: functions, arguments and return values

questions.prompt: You must check, for millions of incoming records, whether record_id was already seen in a batch of 1,000,000 known IDs. Which structure fits best?

options.text: A set of the known IDs.
A list of the known IDs.
options.explanation: Membership in a list scans it: linear time per lookup.

options.text: A tuple of the known IDs.
options.explanation: Also a linear scan; immutability does not speed up lookup.

options.text: A string that concatenates all IDs.
options.explanation: Substring search is slow and can produce false matches.

questions.explanation: Set membership uses hashing and takes constant time on average; a list or tuple lookup takes time proportional to its length.

questions.prompt: Which values can be used as dictionary keys? Select all that apply.

options.text: frozenset({"NO", "CH"})

options.explanation: Lists are mutable and not hashable.

options.text: {"country": "NO"}
options.explanation: Dictionaries are mutable and not hashable.

questions.explanation: Keys must be hashable. Tuples of hashable values and frozensets are; lists, dicts and sets are not.

options.explanation: A generator cannot be restarted.
The blank line is stripped to "" and skipped.

options.text: A StopIteration error on the second list(g).
options.explanation: list() handles exhaustion; it simply returns an empty list.

questions.explanation: A generator is a one-shot iterator. Once exhausted it yields nothing; call the generator function again to iterate again.

questions.prompt: A loader parses an amount field. Bad values must go to a quarantine table while valid rows continue. Which handler fits?

options.text: except: pass
options.explanation: A bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and silently loses the record.

options.text: except Exception: continue
options.explanation: Too broad, and the bad value and reason are lost.

options.text: except (TypeError, ValueError) as exc: send the raw value, the error text and the run ID to quarantine.
No try at all, so the first bad value stops the batch.
options.explanation: Valid when any bad record must stop the run, but this scenario asks for quarantine.

questions.explanation: Catch the narrowest exceptions you expect, keep the original value and reason, and let unexpected programming errors surface.

options.text: run.rows = 5 on an existing instance raises dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError.
JobRun(job_id="j1", rows="ten") raises TypeError because rows is annotated as int.
options.explanation: Annotations are not enforced at runtime; validate external data explicitly.

options.text: Two instances with equal field values compare equal.
frozen=True also makes a list stored in a field immutable.
options.explanation: Freezing is shallow: a contained list can still be mutated.

questions.explanation: A frozen dataclass blocks attribute assignment and generates __eq__ (and __hash__), but it neither checks types nor deep-freezes contents.

questions.prompt: Why pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly when reading a JSON or CSV file in a pipeline?

options.text: Without it, the default text encoding can depend on the platform and Python configuration, so the same file may decode differently on another machine.
JSON files must be read as Latin-1 unless told otherwise.
options.explanation: JSON exchanged between systems is normally UTF-8.

options.text: It makes reading significantly faster.
options.explanation: It is about correctness and reproducibility, not speed.

options.text: It validates the structure of the JSON document.
options.explanation: Decoding text and validating structure are separate steps.

questions.explanation: Serialization is an I/O boundary: fix the encoding, decode, validate the structure, then transform.

links.label: Review: JSON, CSV and file boundaries

questions.prompt:
s = pd.Series(["3", "x", None])
out = pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce").astype("Int64")

What is out?

options.text: 3, <NA>, <NA> with dtype Int64
3, 0, 0 with dtype int64
options.explanation: Coercion produces missing values, not zeros.

options.text: A ValueError because "x" is not numeric.
options.explanation: errors="coerce" turns unparsable values into NaN instead of raising.

options.text: 3.0, NaN, NaN with dtype float64
options.explanation: That is the intermediate result before astype("Int64").

questions.explanation: to_numeric with errors="coerce" yields float64 with NaN; the nullable Int64 dtype keeps integers and shows missing values as <NA>. A value with a fractional part, such as "2.5", would make the cast fail.

links.label: Review: missing data and nullable dtypes
